title: Portland Cement Concrete (PCC)
desc: Concrete is a mineral composite; it is not one single material, but a mixture of components where cement acts as the binder, while sand and gravel make up most of the volume.

title: Portland Cement
desc: The powder binder that, when combined with water, initiates a chemical reaction called hydration to bind sand and aggregates.

title: Limestone (CaCO3)
desc: The most important raw material, mainly consisting of calcium carbonate. It is heated and chemically transformed during production.

title: Hydration Reactions
desc: The chemical reaction triggered when water is added to cement, hardening the paste and binding aggregates into a solid material.

title: Carbonation (Phase 3)
desc: Over time, Ca(OH)2 reacts with CO2 to form CaCO3 + H2O. This lowers internal pH and creates vulnerability to chloride-induced depassivation of reinforcing steel.

title: Tensile Brittleness
desc: Concrete provides high compressive strength (20–50 MPa) but very low tensile strength (approx. 10% of compressive capacity), making it brittle and prone to cracking under tension.

title: Quarrying & Crushing
desc: Large quarries extract limestone, clay, and sand using heavy machinery; crushers break large rocks down prior to processing.

title: Rotary Kiln (1450C)
desc: Temperatures reach approximately 1450C, chemically transforming minerals to form clinker. This stage is energy-intensive, requiring 3.2–3.5 GJ of thermal energy per tonne.

title: Clinker
desc: Small, hard, grey/black stones formed in the kiln; it must be rapidly cooled and ground into an extremely fine powder.

title: Steel Reinforcement
desc: Resolves concrete's tensile weakness by creating a composite system. Hardening around the steel's ribs creates strong mechanical interlock.

title: SCMs (Fly Ash / GGBS)
desc: Industrial by-products like Ground Granulated Blast-furnace Slag (iron) and Fly Ash (coal) that partially replace clinker to reduce environmental impact.

title: Aspdin's Patent (1824)
desc: Joseph Aspdin patented Portland cement in 1824, emerging within Britain's existing network of mechanized manufacturing and transportation.

title: Infrastructures of Control
desc: Cement became connected to the expansion of the industrial state, highly valuable for ports, docks, railways, and military installations to control territories.

title: The Developmental State
desc: Rapidly driven by reconstruction, concrete suited large social-housing programs and infrastructure capable of being standardized at enormous scales across both capitalist and socialist blocs.

title: Multinational Corporations
desc: Previously state-owned cement industries were merged into transnational networks; by 2003, the top five companies controlled ~42% of the global market outside China.

title: Carbon Geopolitics
desc: Because calcination chemically releases CO2, even decarbonizing fuels won't eliminate emissions, creating a new political economy of carbon taxes and emissions trading.

title: Embodied Carbon
desc: The calcination process accounts for about 80% of volume and about 60% of CO2 emissions.

title: Demolition Waste
desc: The biggest end-of-life waste stream is concrete rubble; elements must be separated from contaminants like wood, plastic, and reinforcement steel.

title: Recycled Concrete Aggregate
desc: Crushed concrete (RCA) can be used as road base or hardcore, but old mortar alters water absorption and strength when incorporated into new concrete.

title: Visible Reflectance
desc: PCC typically has a grey appearance with indicative visible-light reflectance of ~40% for smooth surfaces. Wetting reduces reflectance, while carbonation can whiten it.

title: Thermal Mass Storage
desc: Concrete absorbs, stores, and releases heat over time, meaning a surface may feel cool in shade but warm after heating.

title: Acoustic Density
desc: High material density yields excellent sound insulation and airborne noise reduction, but creates a hard, acoustically reflective surface contributing to reverberation.
